source_text: ἀλλ᾿ ὡς καὶ προφῆται προεῖπον, ἀπὸ παρθένου. κατ᾿ ἐπαγγελίαν σημείου γεννώσης τὸν ἐπώνυμον πράγματος, δηλοῦντος ὅτι ἐπὶ τῇ γενέσει αὐτοῦ μετ᾿ ἀνθρώπων ἔσται θεός. Καὶ οἰκεῖόν γε φαίνεταί μοι πρὸς τὴν τοῦ Ἰουδαίου προσωποποιΐαν παραθέσθαι τὴν τοῦ Ἡσαΐου προφητείαν, λέγουσαν ἐκ παρθένου τεχθήσεσθαι τὸν Ἐμμανουήλ· ἣν οὐκ ἐξέθετο, εἴτε μὴ ἐπιστάμενος ὁ πάντ᾿ ἐπαγγελλόμενος εἰδέναι Κέλσος εἴτ᾿ ἀναγνοὺς μὲν ἑκὼν δὲ σιωπήσας, ἵνα μὴ δοκοίη κατασκευάζειν ἄκων τὸν λόγον ἐναντιούμενον αὐτοῦ τῇ προαιρέσει. ἔχει δ᾿ οὕτως ἡ λέξις· „καὶ προσέθετο κύριος τῷ Ἄχαζ λέγων· αἴτησαι σεαυτῷ σημεῖον παρὰ κυρίου θεοῦ σου εἰς βάθος ἢ εἰς ὕψος. καὶ εἶπεν Ἄχαζ· οὐ μὴ αἰτήσω οὐδ᾿ οὐ μὴ πειράσω τὸν κύριον. (καὶ εἶπεν·) ἀκούσατε δὴ, οἶκος Δαυὶδ, μὴ μικρὸν ὑμῖν ἀγῶνα παρέχειν ἀνθρώποις, καὶ πῶς κυρίῳ παρέχετε ἀγῶνα; διὰ τοῦτο δώσει κύριος αὐτὸς ὑμῖν σημεῖον· ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται καὶ τέξεται υἱὸν, καὶ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἐμμανουὴλ“, ὅπερ ἑρμηνεύεται „μεθ᾿ ἡμῶν ὁ θεός“. ὅτι δὲ κακουργῶν ὁ Κέλσος οὐκ ἐξέθετο τὴν προφητείαν, δῆλόν μοι γίνεται ἐκ τοῦ παραθέμενον αὐτὸν πολλὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ Ματθαῖον εὐαγγελίου, ὥσπερ τὸν ἀνατείλαντα ἀστέρα ἐπὶ τῇ γενέσει τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ ἄλλα τῶν παραδόξων, μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν τούτου ἐμνημονευκέναι. ἐὰν δὲ Ἰουδαῖος εὑρεσιλογῶν τὸ „ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος“ μὴ γεγράφθαι λέγῃ ἀλλ᾿ ἀντ᾿ αὐτοῦ „ἰδοὺ ἡ νεᾶνις“, φήσομεν πρὸς αὐτὸν ὅτι ἡ μὲν λέξις ἡ ἀαλμὰ, ἣν οἱ μὲν ἑβδομήκοντα μετειλήφασι πρὸς τὴν παρθένον ἄλλοι δ᾿ εἰς τὴν νεᾶνιν, κεῖται, ὥς φασι, καὶ ἐν τᾷ Δευτερονομίῳ ἐπὶ παρθένου, οὕτως ἔχουσα·„ἐὰν δὲ γένηται παῖς παρθένος μεμνηστευμένη ἀνδρὶ, καὶ εὑρὼν αὐτὴν ἄνθρωπος ἐν πόλει κοιμηθῇ μετ᾿ αὐτῆς, καὶ ἐξάξετε ἀμφοτέρους ἐπὶ τὴν πύλην τῆς πόλεως αὐτῶν, καὶ λιθοβοληθήσονται λίθοις, καὶ ἀποθανοῦνται· τὴν νεᾶνιν ἐπὶ λόγου, διότι οὐκ ἐβόησεν ἐν τῇ πόλει, καὶ τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐπὶ λόγου, διότι ἐταπείνωσε τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ πλησίον αὐτοῦ·“ καὶ ἑξῆς· „ἐὰν δὲ ἐν πεδίῳ εὕρῃ ἄνθρωπος τὴν παῖδα τὴν μεμνηστευμένην καὶ βιασάμενος αὐτὴν ὁ ἄνθρωπος κοιμηθῇ μετ᾿ αὐτῆς, ἀποκτενεῖτε τὸν ἄνθρωπον τὸν κοιμώμενον μετ᾿ αὐτῆς μόνον, καὶ τῇ νεάνιδι οὐ ποιήσετε οὐδέν· οὐκ ἔστι τῇ νεάνιδι ἁμάρτημα θανάτου.“
pass_a_gloss: But as also prophets spoke beforehand, from a virgin. According to a promise of a sign, the one giving birth to the one named after the thing, showing that God will be with men at his birth. And it seems to me to be fitting to set forth the prophecy of Isaiah in relation to the personification of the Jew, saying that Emmanuel will be born from a virgin; which Celsus did not expound, either because he did not know, although he promises to know all things, or because he read it but deliberately kept silent, so that he might not seem to be constructing against his will the argument opposing his preference. The passage has the following wording: 'And the Lord added to Ahaz, saying, Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, either into the depths or into the heights. And Ahaz said, I will not ask and I will not test the Lord.' And he said, 'Hear now, house of David, is it not enough for you to make people tired, and how do you make the Lord tired? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, the virgin will conceive in the womb and will give birth to a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel', which is interpreted as 'God with us'. That Celsus, acting wickedly, did not expound the prophecy is clear to me from the fact that he passed over many things from the Gospel according to Matthew, such as the star rising at the birth of Jesus and other remarkable things, and did not even mention the beginning of it. But if a Jew, making a discovery, says that 'behold, the virgin' is not written but instead 'behold, the young woman', we will say to him that the phrase 'almah', which the Seventy translators rendered as 'parthenos' (virgin) and others as 'neanis' (young woman), is also found in Deuteronomy concerning a virgin, having the following wording: 'If a virgin betrothed to a man is found, and a man finds her in a city and sleeps with her, and you bring out both of them to the gate of their city, and stone them with stones, and they will die; the young woman because she did not cry out in the city, and the man because he humbled the wife of his neighbor'; and next: 'If a man finds the betrothed young woman in a field and rapes her, and the man sleeps with her, you will kill the man who slept with her alone, and to the young woman you will do nothing; there is no sin of death for the young woman'.
pass_b_english: But the prophets also spoke beforehand: he would be born from a virgin. In fulfillment of a promised sign, the one who gives birth to the one named after the reality he embodies shows that God will be with human beings at his birth. (Isaiah 7:10-14) It seems fitting to me to set forth the prophecy of Isaiah in response to the Jew's personification, which declares that Emmanuel will be born from a virgin. Celsus did not expound this passage—whether because he did not know it, despite his claim to know everything, or because he read it but deliberately kept silent, so as not to appear to be building against his will the argument that opposes his own preference. The text runs as follows: 'And the Lord spoke again to Ahaz, saying, "Ask a sign for yourself from the Lord your God, either in the depths or in the heights." And Ahaz said, "I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test." Then he said, "Hear now, house of David: is it too little for you to weary people, that you also weary my Lord? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, the virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel," which is interpreted "God with us." (Isaiah 7:10-14) That Celsus, acting wickedly, passed over this prophecy is clear to me from the fact that he omitted many things from the Gospel according to Matthew—for instance, the star that rose at the birth of Jesus and other remarkable events—and did not even mention the beginning of that Gospel. If a Jew, making a clever objection, says that "behold, the virgin" is not written but rather "behold, the young woman," we will answer him that the Hebrew word almah, which the Seventy translators rendered as parthenos (virgin) and others as neanis (young woman), also occurs in Deuteronomy with reference to a virgin, in the following wording: "If a virgin betrothed to a man is found, and a man finds her in a city and lies with her, you shall bring both of them out to the gate of that city and stone them to death with stones; the young woman because she did not cry out in the city, and the man because he violated his neighbor's wife." (Deuteronomy 22:23-24) And next: "If a man finds the betrothed young woman in the open country and seizes her and lies with her, you shall kill only the man who lay with her, but you shall do nothing to the young woman; there is no capital offense for the young woman." (Deuteronomy 22:25-27)

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Greek text, including the nuances of the 'almah' argument and the specific legal language of Deuteronomy. Scripture citations in Pass B correctly identify the quoted passages (Isaiah 7:10-14 and Deuteronomy 22:23-27) which were alluded to in the Greek. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source.
